judgements.justification: Five of six picks are excellent for a general listener—Wikipedia articles on sensation novels, coverture, the Married Women's Property Act, and No Name itself provide accessible context, plus Ackroyd's biography of Collins is a findable trade book; only the Barbara Bodichon entry, while relevant to women's rights, is somewhat tangential to understanding the novel itself.

Mixed picks: three solid accessible books (Gérin's biography, Miller's Victorian sexualities intro, and Wadsö-Lecaros on governesses) would genuinely help a listener, but Kanwit's academic study on art criticism and Carroll's queer theory monograph are more specialized/niche, and the list lacks contextual breadth (no Gaskell biography alternatives, no general Victorian novel guides, nothing on small-town life or Cheshire setting).

Five of six picks are excellent and accessible (Charles Dickens biography, two London histories, Victorian historical fiction, and Victorian sexualities), but the Court of Chancery Wikipedia article, while relevant to the novel's legal satire, is somewhat narrow and technical for a general listener seeking broader illumination.

The picks offer genuine historical context (Victorian era economics, poverty documentation) relevant to Our Mutual Friend's themes, but ref-9 and ref-13 are academic monographs from the 1950s-1902s that may be harder for a general listener to locate, while ref-18 (London Labour and the London Poor) is an excellent accessible primary source; the selection lacks literary criticism directly addressing Dickens's novel itself.

Four solid picks (Oliphant biography, Victorian sexuality overview, historical fiction forms, and the novel's Wikipedia entry) are accessible and directly relevant, but ref-26 on Miss Marjoribanks, while useful for understanding Oliphant's other work, is less central to understanding Hester specifically than a literary biography or critical study of the novel itself would be.

Four solid, accessible picks (Chesterton's Victorian literature overview, Shaw on historical fiction forms, the governess novel context, and George Eliot biography) that would genuinely help a listener, though the Zionism Wikipedia entry is somewhat tangential to the novel's primary concerns and could have been replaced with more directly relevant material on Eliot's Jewishness or the novel's Jewish themes.

Four strong, accessible picks (Chesterton on Victorian literature, Shaw on historical fiction, Wadsö-Lecaros on the governess novel, and the George Eliot Wikipedia article) that would genuinely help a listener, though the Zionism article is somewhat tangential to the novel's core concerns and the picks could have included more on Eliot herself or the Jewish themes.

The picks include one inaccessible dissertation (ref-27), one specialized book on Victorian sexuality that may miss Cranford's specific themes (ref-18), and several academic articles/chapters (ref-23, ref-45) that won't help a general listener; missing are obvious accessible picks like the Gaskell biography (ref-16, which was selected but is the only solid choice), Wikipedia on Gaskell/Cranford (ref-7, ref-9), or other biographies, leaving the list skewed toward specialist scholarship.
